title: The Need of Scripture, as a Guide and Teacher, in Coming to God as a Creator
sectionSummaries: 1. God gives his elect a better help to the knowledge of himself—viz. the Holy Scriptures. This he did from the very first.

2. First, By oracles and visions, and the ministry of the Patriarchs. Secondly, By the promulgation of the Law, and the preaching of the Prophets. Why the doctrines of religion are committed to writing.

3. This view confirmed, 1. By the depravity of our nature making it necessary in every one who would know God to have recourse to the word; 2. From those passages of the Psalms in which God is introduced as reigning.
4. Another confirmation from certain direct statements in the Psalms. Lastly, From the words of our Saviour.

paragraphs: Therefore , though the effulgence which is presented to every eye, both in the heavens and on the earth, leaves the ingratitude of man without excuse, since God, in order to bring the whole human race under the same condemnation, holds forth to all, without exception, a mirror of his Deity in his works, another and better help must be given to guide us properly to God as a Creator. Not in vain, therefore, has he added the light of his Word in order that he might make himself known unto salvation, and bestowed the privilege on those whom he was pleased to bring into nearer and more familiar relation to himself. For, seeing how the minds of men were carried to and fro, and found no certain resting-place, he chose the Jews for a peculiar people, and then hedged them in that they might not, like others, go astray. And not in vain does he, by the same means, retain us in his knowledge, since but for this, even those who, in comparison of others, seem to stand strong, would quickly fall away. For as the aged, or those whose sight is defective, when any books however fair, is set before them, though they perceive that there is something written are scarcely able to make out two consecutive words, but, when aided by glasses, begin to read distinctly, so Scripture, gathering together the impressions of Deity, which, till then, lay confused in our minds, dissipates the darkness, and shows us the true God clearly. God therefore bestows a gift of singular value, when, for the instruction of the Church, he employs not dumb teachers merely, but opens his own sacred mouth; when he not only proclaims that some God must be worshipped, but at the same time declares that He is the God to whom worship is due; when he not only teaches his elect to have respect to God, but manifests himself as the God to whom this respect should be paid.

The course which God followed towards his Church from the very first, was to supplement these common proofs by the addition of his Word, as a surer and more direct means of discovering himself. And there can be no doubt that it was by this help, Adam, Noah, Abraham, and the other patriarchs, attained to that familiar knowledge which, in a manner, distinguished them from unbelievers. I am not now speaking of the peculiar doctrines of faith by which they were elevated to the hope of eternal blessedness. It was necessary, in passing from death unto life, that they should know God, not only as a Creator, but as a Redeemer also; and both kinds of knowledge they certainly did obtain from the Word. In point of order, however, the knowledge first given was that which made them acquainted with the God by whom the world was made and is governed. To this first knowledge was afterwards added the more intimate knowledge which alone quickens dead souls, and by which God is known not only as the Creator of the worlds and the sole author and disposer of all events, but also as a Redeemer, in the person of the Mediator. But as the fall and the corruption of nature have not yet been considered, I now postpone the consideration of the remedy (for which, see Book 2 c. 6 &c). Let the reader then remember, that I am not now treating of the covenant by which God adopted the children of Abraham, or of that branch of doctrine by which, as founded in Christ, believers have, properly speaking, been in all ages separated from the profane heathen. I am only showing that it is necessary to apply to Scripture, in order to learn the sure marks which distinguish God, as the Creator of the world, from the whole herd of fictitious gods. We shall afterward, in due course, consider the work of Redemption. In the meantime, though we shall adduce many passages from the New Testament, and some also from the Law and the Prophets, in which express mention is made of Christ, the only object will be to show that God, the Maker of the world, is manifested to us in Scripture, and his true character expounded, so as to save us from wandering up and down, as in a labyrinth, in search of some doubtful deity.
Whether God revealed himself to the fathers by oracles and visions, 70 The French adds, “C’est à dire, temoignages celestes;”—that is to say, messages from heaven.
Tertullian, Apologet. adv. Gentes: “Quae plenius et impressius tam ipsum quam dispositiones ejus et voluntates adiremus, instrumentum adjecit literature,” &c.

For if we reflect how prone the human mind is to lapse into forgetfulness of God, how readily inclined to every kind of error, how bent every now and then on devising new and fictitious religions, it will be easy to understand how necessary it was to make such a depository of doctrine as would secure it from either perishing by the neglect, vanishing away amid the errors, or being corrupted by the presumptuous audacity of men. It being thus manifest that God, foreseeing the inefficiency of his image imprinted on the fair form of the universe, has given the assistance of his Word to all whom he has ever been pleased to instruct effectually, we, too, must pursue this straight path, if we aspire in earnest to a genuine contemplation of God;—we must go, I say, to the Word, where the character of God, drawn from his works is described accurately and to the life; these works being estimated, not by our depraved Judgment, but by the standard of eternal truth. If, as I lately said, we turn aside from it, how great soever the speed with which we move, we shall never reach the goal, because we are off the course. We should consider that the brightness of the Divine countenance, which even an apostle declares to be inaccessible ( 1 Tim. 6:16 ), is a kind of labyrinth,—a labyrinth to us inextricable, if the Word do not serve us as a thread to guide our path; and that it is better to limp in the way, than run with the greatest swiftness out of it. Hence the Psalmist, after repeatedly declaring ( Psalm 93, 96, 97, 99 , &c). that superstition should be banished from the world in order that pure religion may flourish, introduces God as reigning ; meaning by the term, not the power which he possesses and which he exerts in the government of universal nature, but the doctrine by which he maintains his due supremacy: because error never can be eradicated from the heart of man until the true knowledge of God has been implanted in it.

Accordingly, the same prophet, after mentioning that the heavens declare the glory of God, that the firmament sheweth forth the works of his hands, that the regular succession of day and night proclaim his Majesty, proceeds to make mention of the Word:—“The law of the Lord,” says he, “is perfect, converting the soul; the testimony of the Lord is sure, making wise the simple. The statutes of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart; the commandment of the Lord is pure, enlightening the eyes,” ( Psalm 19:1-9 ). For though the law has other uses besides (as to which, see Book 2 c. 7, sec. 6, 10, 12), the general meaning is, that it is the proper school for training the children of God; the invitation given to all nations, to behold him in the heavens and earth, proving of no avail. The same view is taken in the 29th Psalm, where the Psalmist, after discoursing on the dreadful voice of God, which, in thunder, wind, rain, whirlwind, and tempest, shakes the earth, makes the mountains tremble, and breaks the cedars, concludes by saying, “that in his temple does every one speak of his glory,” unbelievers being deaf to all God’s words when they echo in the air. In like manner another Psalm, after describing the raging billows of the sea, thus concludes, “Thy testimonies are very sure; holiness becometh thine house for ever,” ( Psalm 93:5 ). To the same effect are the words of our Saviour to the Samaritan woman, when he told her that her nation and all other nations worshipped they knew not what; and that the Jews alone gave worship to the true God ( John 4:22 ). Since the human mind, through its weakness, was altogether unable to come to God if not aided and upheld by his sacred word, it necessarily followed that all mankind, the Jews excepted, inasmuch as they sought God without the Word, were labouring under vanity and error.

application: Calvin's point here is plain and bracing — the works of creation leave every man without excuse, yet they cannot lead us home; for that, God adds his Word, the spectacles through which dim eyes finally read his true character clearly. A faithless age tells us the divine is whatever the sunset stirs in us, and many who name Christ drift on that same current, content with a God they have felt but never heard. We are not. The Lord did not leave his Church to grope after a doubtful deity in the labyrinth of her own impressions; he opened his sacred mouth, and the family that would know him must go where he has spoken. So gather your household to Scripture, not to vague spirituality — read it at the table, bind it on your children, let it correct what nature only hints. The heavens declare his glory, but his Word converts the soul; keep your feet on that straight path, for it is better to limp in the way than to run swiftly out of it.

paragraphs: The brightness that meets every eye, both in the heavens and on the earth, leaves the ingratitude of mankind without excuse. To bring the whole human race under the same condemnation, God holds out to all people, without exception, a mirror of his deity in his works. Even so, another and better help must be given to guide us rightly to God as our Creator. It was not in vain, then, that he added the light of his Word, so that he might make himself known to us for our salvation. He granted this privilege to those whom he was pleased to bring into a nearer and more familiar relationship with himself. For he saw how the minds of people were carried back and forth, finding no sure resting place. So he chose the Jews as a people set apart, and then fenced them in, so that they might not wander off into error as others had done. And it is not in vain that, by this same means, he keeps us in the knowledge of himself. For without it, even those who seem to stand strong in comparison with others would quickly fall away. Consider the elderly, or those whose eyesight is failing. When a beautiful book is set before them, they can tell that something is written there, yet they can barely make out two words in a row. But once they are helped by glasses, they begin to read clearly. In the same way, Scripture gathers together the impressions of God's deity, which until then lay confused in our minds. It scatters the darkness and shows us the true God clearly. God therefore gives a gift of singular value when, for the instruction of the Church, he uses not silent teachers only, but opens his own sacred mouth. He does more than proclaim that some god must be worshiped: he declares that he is the God to whom worship is due. He does more than teach his chosen people to regard God: he reveals himself as the God they are to regard.

From the very beginning, this was the way God dealt with his Church: he supplemented these common proofs by adding his Word, as a surer and more direct means of disclosing himself. And there can be no doubt that it was by this help that Adam, Noah, Abraham, and the other patriarchs reached that intimate knowledge which, in a sense, set them apart from unbelievers. I am not speaking now of the particular doctrines of faith that lifted them up to the hope of eternal blessedness. In passing from death to life, they had to know God not only as Creator but also as Redeemer, and both kinds of knowledge they certainly received from the Word. In order, however, the knowledge first given was the kind that made them acquainted with the God by whom the world was made and is governed. To this first knowledge was later added the deeper knowledge which alone brings dead souls to life. By it God is known not only as the Creator of all things and the sole author and disposer of all that happens, but also as a Redeemer, in the person of the Mediator. But since the fall and the corruption of our nature have not yet been considered, I will set aside the question of the remedy for now (for that, see Book 2, chapter 6 and following). So let the reader remember that I am not now dealing with the covenant by which God adopted the children of Abraham, nor with that branch of teaching by which believers, grounded in Christ, have in every age been properly set apart from the ungodly nations. I am only showing that we must turn to Scripture in order to learn the sure marks that distinguish God, the Creator of the world, from the whole crowd of made-up gods. We will consider the work of redemption later, in its proper place. Meanwhile, though we will bring forward many passages from the New Testament, and some from the Law and the Prophets as well, in which Christ is expressly mentioned, our only aim will be to show that God, the Maker of the world, is revealed to us in Scripture, and that his true character is set forth there, so that we are not left wandering up and down, as in a maze, searching for some uncertain deity.
Whether God revealed himself to the fathers by oracles and visions (that is to say, by testimonies from heaven),

Tertullian, in his Apology against the Nations, writes that, so that we might approach more fully and more deeply both God himself and his arrangements and his will, he added the instrument of Scripture, and so on.

If we consider how easily the human mind slips into forgetfulness of God, how readily it is drawn toward every kind of error, and how it leans, again and again, toward inventing new and made-up religions, it becomes easy to see how necessary it was to establish a storehouse of doctrine. Such a record would keep that teaching from perishing through neglect, from fading away amid our errors, or from being corrupted by the reckless boldness of people. It is plain, then, that God, foreseeing that the image he had stamped on the beautiful form of the universe would not be enough, has given the help of his Word to all whom he has ever been pleased to teach effectively. We too must follow this straight path, if we genuinely long for a true vision of God. We must go, I say, to the Word, where the character of God, drawn from his works, is described accurately and to the life. There his works are weighed not by our corrupt judgment, but by the standard of eternal truth. If we turn aside from the Word, then no matter how fast we move, we will never reach the goal, because we are off the course. We should bear in mind that the brightness of God's face, which even an apostle calls unapproachable (1 Timothy 6:16), is a kind of maze, a maze we cannot escape unless the Word serves as a thread to guide our way. It is better to limp along the right path than to run with great speed off of it. So the Psalmist, after repeatedly declaring (in Psalms 93, 96, 97, 99, and others) that superstition must be banished from the world so that pure religion may flourish, presents God as reigning. By that word he means not the power God possesses and exercises in governing all of nature, but the teaching by which he upholds his rightful supremacy. For error can never be rooted out of the human heart until the true knowledge of God has been planted in it.

So the same prophet, after saying that the heavens declare the glory of God, that the sky shows forth the work of his hands, and that the steady succession of day and night proclaims his majesty, goes on to speak of the Word. "The law of the Lord," he says, "is perfect, converting the soul; the testimony of the Lord is sure, making wise the simple. The statutes of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart; the commandment of the Lord is pure, enlightening the eyes" (Psalm 19:1-9). For although the law serves other purposes as well (on which see Book 2, chapter 7, sections 6, 10, and 12), its general meaning is that it is the proper school for training the children of God. The invitation given to all nations to behold him in the heavens and the earth proved of no use. The same view appears in Psalm 29, where the Psalmist, after speaking of the dreadful voice of God, which in thunder, wind, rain, whirlwind, and storm shakes the earth, makes the mountains tremble, and breaks the cedars, ends by saying that in his temple everyone speaks of his glory. Unbelievers, meanwhile, are deaf to all God's words when they ring out in the open air. In the same way, another Psalm, after describing the raging waves of the sea, concludes, "Your testimonies are very sure; holiness becomes your house forever" (Psalm 93:5). The words of our Savior to the Samaritan woman point the same way, when he told her that her nation and all other nations worshiped what they did not know, and that the Jews alone gave worship to the true God (John 4:22). Since the human mind, in its weakness, was wholly unable to come to God unless helped and held up by his sacred Word, it followed of necessity that all people, except the Jews, were toiling in emptiness and error, because they sought God apart from the Word.
